Keywords: Ashenda, Shandar, Anatolia

outputs.L1:
So I go to Ashenda to get some fix: Shandar is there, playing his lute, and a dark-haired angel is combing a violin. I cry, “Anatolia! Anatolia!” I’m a nightingale shrieking at dawn’s first flick; I’m the unknown soldier singing, “It’s me again.” I say, “One more, and I’m ready for the Western World.”

Then I’m at a bar with Lucinda, and we’re drooling over the body, over discipline and the reign of Robespierre. Then it’s consummation time, and I say, “Hey, there’s a ram butting at the door, and a widow’s crying for something.” I say, “Lucinda, I’ve got a drum in my belly,” and she says, “I’m a goddamn shivering eel.”

Then it’s polka on a South Dakota lawn: Shandar doodling, Shahrazad stomping by the window, soaking up the light. Then we all smoke Camels, and Lucinda says, “I wish I could live without having to disown.” And I say, “Yeah—tell me more about that.”
outputs.L2:
I head to Ashenda looking for a fix. Shandar is there, plucking his lute, while a dark-haired angel draws music from a violin. “Anatolia! Anatolia!” I shout. I become a nightingale screaming at the first glimmer of day, then the unknown soldier announcing through song that I have returned. I ask for one more, saying that afterward I’ll be prepared for the Western World.

Next, Lucinda and I are in a bar, salivating over the body, discipline, and Robespierre’s rule. When the moment of consummation arrives, I point out a ram pounding its horns against the door and a widow weeping in need. I tell Lucinda there is a drum beating inside my stomach; she replies that she is a damn eel trembling all over.

Then the scene shifts to a polka on a lawn in South Dakota. Shandar idly sketches Shahrazad as she stamps past the window, drinking in the sunlight. Afterward, everyone smokes Camels. Lucinda says she longs to live without being forced to disown, and I answer, “Yes—say more about that.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker visits Ashenda, where music shapes the atmosphere of the evening. Shandar plays the lute, while a dark-haired woman accompanies him on the violin. Deeply moved by their performance, the speaker invokes Anatolia and drifts into a series of imaginative transformations, envisioning himself first as a nightingale and then as an unknown soldier.

Later, at a bar with Lucinda, his thoughts turn toward the discipline imposed upon the body and the historical terror associated with the reign of Robespierre. These reflections mingle politics, history, and physical experience, giving the encounter an uneasy intensity.

During a more intimate moment, the speaker and Lucinda communicate through surreal and shifting images. A battering ram appears beside the figure of a crying widow; the body becomes a belly drum and then a shivering eel. These strange metaphors convey both desire and vulnerability, suggesting that their closeness cannot be expressed in ordinary language.

The group eventually gathers on a lawn in South Dakota, where they dance, smoke Camels, and continue their conversation. Amid this relaxed but dreamlike scene, Lucinda expresses her wish to live without being forced to disown any part of herself or her experience. Her desire brings the episode’s scattered images together, emphasizing a longing for freedom, acceptance, and an undivided life.
outputs.L4:
The speaker recounts a surreal and fragmented journey shaped by music, desire, memory, and cultural displacement. Rather than unfolding as a linear narrative, the experience moves through abrupt changes of place and mood, passing from the celebration of Ashenda to Anatolia, from the charged intimacy of a bar to the distant landscape of South Dakota. These settings overlap as if they belong to a dream, linked less by geography than by rhythm, emotion, and association. Music carries the speaker across boundaries, while historical references and flashes of sensuality blur the distinction between personal memory and collective experience.

The rapid shifts create an atmosphere of exhilaration, but they also suggest instability. Each place offers a temporary scene of connection, yet none becomes a secure home. Celebration and desire promise release, while history repeatedly intrudes, reminding the speaker that identities are shaped by migration, conflict, inheritance, and loss. Ashenda evokes communal ritual and cultural continuity; Anatolia introduces another landscape marked by layered histories; the bar becomes a space of performance and fleeting intimacy; and South Dakota appears both geographically remote and emotionally charged. Together, these locations form a fractured map of belonging.

Lucinda stands at the emotional center of this movement. Her wish to live without “having to disown” gives the dreamlike journey its deepest meaning. The phrase suggests more than a refusal to reject a particular place, people, or past. It expresses a desire to exist without dividing the self—to embrace one identity without betraying another, to enter the present without erasing history, and to seek freedom without surrendering attachment. In a world where cultural and personal identities are often treated as incompatible, Lucinda longs for a form of belonging that does not demand denial.

The text’s ecstatic energy therefore carries an undercurrent of sorrow. Music, dancing, travel, and erotic attraction create moments in which boundaries seem to dissolve, but those moments cannot entirely overcome alienation. The speaker’s fragmented movement reflects the difficulty of making a coherent self from scattered histories and places. Yet the fragmentation also opens imaginative possibilities: if identity cannot be contained within a single location or tradition, it may be created through connection, memory, and desire. Ultimately, the journey becomes a search for a home capacious enough to hold contradiction—a way of living in which no part of oneself must be abandoned in order to belong.
outputs.L5:
### Ashenda and Shandar: A Tale from Anatolia

Across the vast landscapes of Anatolia, where ancient roads wind between mountains and fertile plains, countless cultures have met and left their mark. In a small village along one of these forgotten routes lived two young travelers named Ashenda and Shandar.

Ashenda carried songs from distant lands. Her name recalled the joyful Ashenda festival celebrated in northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, when girls and young women gather in colorful clothing to sing, dance, and honor community traditions. Shandar, meanwhile, was a storyteller fascinated by Anatolia’s layered history—from Hittite cities and Greek temples to Seljuk caravanserais and Ottoman towns.

Together, they journeyed through Anatolia, sharing music and stories wherever they stopped. In Cappadocia, their voices echoed among the rock-cut churches. On the plains of central Anatolia, Shandar told legends beside the fire while Ashenda taught villagers the rhythms of her homeland.

Their travels became a symbol of cultural connection. Although Ashenda’s traditions originated far from Anatolia, her songs found new meaning there. Through friendship, music, and storytelling, Ashenda and Shandar showed that distant cultures can meet without losing their unique identities—and that every road can become a bridge between worlds.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal stream-of-consciousness prose poem about Ashenda, Shandar, and Lucinda, using ampersands instead of “and” and almost no punctuation.
counterfactuals.output:
Ashenda wakes inside a blue pomegranate & hears the moon sewing silver ladders into her hair

Shandar walks backward through a field of sleeping mirrors carrying a small red thunderstorm beneath his tongue

Lucinda is already everywhere

she is the milk in the bell  
the bell in the bird  
the bird dreaming it is a door

Ashenda calls out & her voice becomes seven white horses running across the ceiling of the sea

Shandar opens his mouth & the storm crawls free wearing tiny boots

Lucinda laughs & all the clocks forget their numbers

they meet where the river folds itself into a paper boat & the paper boat folds itself into a moth & the moth enters Ashenda’s eye

inside her eye Shandar is building a palace from salt & Lucinda is teaching the windows to breathe

no one remembers who arrived first

perhaps the pomegranate

perhaps the thunder

perhaps the soft green silence growing between their shadows

Ashenda takes Shandar by the echo

Shandar takes Lucinda by the flame

Lucinda takes Ashenda by the dream

& together they drift beyond morning where the sky has no floor & every star is a mouth whispering their names into the dark bright water
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a breathless dream narrative that blends Anatolia, Robespierre, South Dakota, musical instruments, cigarettes, romance, and war imagery.
counterfactuals.output: I dreamed Anatolia was unrolling beneath us like a scorched carpet, all poppies and cavalry dust, while Robespierre stood on a minaret tuning a silver violin and shouting that virtue was only terror in love with the moon, and you, wearing a South Dakota rodeo jacket, pressed a cigarette to my lips though neither of us smoked, and the ember flared like a tiny besieged city as drums thundered beyond the wheat, trumpets answered from trenches full of blue snow, and we ran hand in hand past abandoned cannons, broken lutes, and horses draped in wedding veils, ran until Ankara became the Badlands and the Badlands became a ballroom where soldiers waltzed with ghosts, while Robespierre descended through the ceiling on a parachute of red silk, demanding silence for the execution of dawn, but the saxophones rebelled, the cellos opened fire, cymbals flashed like sabers, and you kissed me with tobacco and rain on your breath as the whole horizon charged toward us—bayonets, sunflowers, banners, buffalo—until war collapsed into music, music into smoke, smoke into your hair, and I woke still running, still kissing you, still hearing somewhere between Mount Ararat and Rapid City the last impossible note trembling above the guns.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental Beat-style monologue in one paragraph, featuring a lute-playing man, a dark-haired violinist, a mysterious woman named Lucinda, and bizarre animal metaphors.
counterfactuals.output: The lute-playing man came limping down the midnight avenue, plucking blue sparks from strings tuned to the weather, while the dark-haired violinist sawed open the moon and let its silver animals tumble shrieking into the gutters—foxes with teacup eyes, pigeons wearing the sorrowful masks of horses, one enormous moth coughing like a courthouse—and there was Lucinda, mysterious Lucinda, leaning beneath the pawnshop sign as if she had been invented by smoke, saying nothing, saying everything, her red shoes full of rain, and brother I tell you the city reared up then like a drunken giraffe in a telephone booth, all knees and static, while the lute man grinned his ruined grin and played the secret chord that makes alley cats remember Atlantis, and the violinist bent lower, hair black as the last page of a burned Bible, bow flashing, blood humming, until Lucinda lifted one gloved hand and every taxi became a yellow beetle praying on its back, every window blinked with owl-hunger, every cop grew antlers of pale bureaucracy, and we ran—yes, we ran—through the saxophone steam and prophetic garbage, following her perfume of oranges and thunderstorms toward the river, where dawn crouched like a pink baboon washing coins, and Lucinda stepped onto the water, laughing softly, while the two musicians played us past reason, past rent, past the iron cages of morning, into that wild green silence where the soul is only a three-legged dog chasing the endless meat wagon of God.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a hallucinatory poem that moves abruptly from a foreign city to a bar, then to an erotic encounter and finally a polka on a suburban lawn.
counterfactuals.output:
In Tangier, the blue doors blinked  
like sleepless gods.  
A donkey carried the moon uphill,  
its hooves striking sparks from Arabic rain.  
Minarets poured silver into my ears—  
then—

I was in a bar in Milwaukee  
where the jukebox coughed up violets  
and every glass contained a tiny storm.  
The bartender had antlers.  
He said, *You’ve missed the last train to yourself,*  
and polished a mirror with my name.

Then your hand—warm semaphore—  
opened the dark beneath my shirt.  
We kissed as if exchanging passports,  
as if the body were a border  
both governments had forgotten.  
Your breath moved over me,  
slow fire through tall grass;  
the room unbuttoned its red walls  
and floated away.

Suddenly: noon.

A suburban lawn. Sprinklers applauding.  
Plastic flamingos tilted toward revelation.  
An accordion wheezed in the hydrangeas  
and we spun into a furious polka—  
barefoot, half-dressed, laughing—  
while neighbors emerged with casseroles,  
while satellites dropped their spoons,  
while the neat white houses danced on their foundations  
and the sun, enormous and checkered,  
counted:

one, two, three—  
one, two, three—  
forever out of time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented, punctuation-light prose poem in the voice of a wandering unknown soldier, ending with a quiet conversation about living without disowning oneself.
counterfactuals.output:
no name on the tag  
no town in the mouth  
only the road folding itself  
under one boot then the other  

I carried a rifle until it became weather  
rain along the shoulder  
iron against sleep  

the fields kept no record  
wheat rose through helmets  
crows lifted from the mouths of cannons  
each village gave me another face  
then took it back  

someone called me brother  
someone called me enemy  
someone washed my hands in a tin basin  
and would not ask  
what color the blood had been  

at night the dead walked beside me  
not accusing  
only tired  
their pockets full of small things  
a button  
a key  
a letter gone soft at the folds  

I had nothing small enough to save  

so I wandered  
past the last checkpoint  
past the burned orchard  
past the map ending in white  

years may have passed  
or one long winter  

sometimes I slept in barns  
sometimes beneath bridges  
sometimes in a room where a child had drawn  
a yellow house  
a blue door  
five birds without wings  

I wanted to enter that house  
I wanted to knock  

but the hand that knocked  
was also the hand that fired  

one evening beside a low fire  
an old woman gave me soup  
and sat without looking at my uniform  

you are alive she said  

I am not sure I answered  

the fire settled  
a little red among the ash  

then live she said  

how  

without leaving yourself behind  

I looked at my hands  

even this self I asked  

even this one she said softly  
especially this one
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
